moves.spoken: First 2000-rated opponent — and against the Sicilian, White reaches for the Alapin.
The quiet c3 — the Alapin — preparing to build a big centre with d4.
Black replies d6, which is not the most testing choice: it lets White seize the centre.
So White grabs it with d4.
Black develops and leans on the e4-pawn.
White defends by developing the bishop to d3 — with a couple of subtleties to keep in mind, especially against the knight to c6.
And there it is, the knight to c6.
White develops the knight to f3, guarding d4. The bishop to g4 would look intimidating here — more on that after the game.
Black chooses the very passive e6.
White castles — nothing special is required against such a quiet setup.
Black develops the bishop to e7. White has two good roads: open the centre with the capture, or play flexibly.
White chooses flexibility with the bishop to g5, developing by the book.

The queen's knight goes to d2 — the one drawback of the Alapin is that it cannot reach c3 — but it is fine here, and it also props up the e4-pawn. White is comfortably better with a lovely pawn centre.
Black strikes with e5. Now the decision many players find hard — capture or push? Taking would open the position in Black's favour and hit the bishop, so...
...White keeps it closed with d5, holding the space advantage, which in theory should tell.
Black jumps the knight to b4.
White retreats the bishop to e2 — but there is a tactical detail here White failed to anticipate.
And Black finds it — the knight takes on d5. White had missed this. But this is the beauty of being positionally better: you can slip and still be fine.
White captures on e7.
Black recaptures — and because the d-file is now open, the question becomes how to pressure the pawn on d6.
The knight to c4, leaning on d6. No disaster — White still has a good game — but this was an instructive mistake in the making.
Black develops the bishop to e6 — and this lets White win the pawn straight back.
White wins it back with the knight on d6, and the position is roughly level. Had Black tried to push, White would take and the e5-pawn would hang — and White has designs on that pawn too.

Black's knight on b4 gives some counterplay. The queen to c7 is not the most accurate — the queen to b6 was better, planning to pile on that knight. Now White has ideas, starting with the knight to b5 with tempo.
Most players would activate the rook to c1, but the real priority is that loose knight — chess is about priorities — so White evacuates it to b5 first.
And now, with the knight safely out and defended, White can do something impossible a moment ago — because Black has forgotten the e5-pawn is hanging.
The knight grabs on e5, and White is up a pawn. Sometimes chess is about resisting the by-the-book move and prioritising instead.
Grabbing on a2 would lose material, so Black plays a6, shooing the knight.
No problem — the knight retreats to c3, an even safer square.
Black brings a rook to d8. White must take care — the queen to e1 would walk into a fork — so the queen goes to a4 instead, staying active and pressing the knights.
In review: Black's d6 hands White the centre — a line worth knowing from both sides.
If Black tries the pin with the bishop to g4, White simply plays d5.
And here a knight to e5 might look strong, but with that diagonal open White has a lovely, typical idea.

The check on b5 is the key — after the bishop blocks, White takes on e5, and when the smoke clears White is up a piece. It is not a queen blunder, it is a setup — and this same trick turns up in countless openings, including a famous Queen's Gambit version.
